ACCESS launched in **April 2011**; the migration completed **without disruption to live payment operations**, and the dashboards became standard operational tooling.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border payments. Matt designed workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, working with the FX team on real-time currency conversion, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and bulk processing. He delivered an implementation blueprint ready for development execution. Revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

At **American Express**, Virtual Payments Platform adoption was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, no sandbox, and testing dependencies. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built secure, virtualized testing environments. His team used Lean Product and XP practices and validated the portal through a Client Onboarding Test Drive. answer_md:
🐾 Here’s where Matt worked on payment engines, global connectivity, and client adoption.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, regional payment systems had different data models, permissions, and compliance records. The bank was building ACCESS Next Generation on Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform, but its requirements went beyond the platform’s out-of-box capabilities.

For client administrators, he replaced individual permission changes with bulk grouping and a centralized dashboard, reducing entitlement management from days to minutes.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, consolidating regional systems into a unified portal serving **135,000+** corporations, financial institutions, governments, and municipalities across **180+ countries**. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for payments across regions.

At **American Express**, Matt’s work addressed a different payments problem: clients struggled to evaluate and integrate its Virtual Payments Platform because SDKs were missing, documentation was fragmented, and there was no sandbox. He co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, created use case-driven API documentation, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, and client onboarding time decreased.

question: What’s his leadership style?

router_real.matched: What's Matt's leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. At **Norfolk Southern**, the balanced-team, test-first approach Matt introduced did not initially hold in day-to-day work.

In early **2020**, his Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, the client reported rising defects even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed with both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, just as the pandemic forced the team into remote work.

Matt had put pairing, test-driven development, and continuous integration in place, but the reinforcement and verification were missing. An engineer was building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete while defects went undetected. The backlog also contained vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done.

Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite, exposed the gaps, and rebuilt the backlog with testable stories. Frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus worked alongside the engineers to redo code and tests through an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

The follow-through changed too. Pairs rotated daily, test cases became an explicit step before implementation, and standups checked that sequence. New engineers paired with seasoned practitioners. During remote work, pairs traded drivers frequently to reduce fatigue and break mental blocks.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. The practices held after the experts left, and the crisis failure mode did not recur. Matt’s stated lesson was that implementing a practice is only half the work: reinforcement, follow-up, and verification had been missing.

🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams executing test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup, but he relied on that documentation rather than verifying the controls. He focused on delivery pressures instead of validating access patterns. He did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception, or verify that production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**. The root cause was insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. He worked with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project, a systemic failure with an individual consequence.

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach. His description of the failure is direct: these were assumptions he should have verified rather than inherited.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s payments work, from payment-engine delivery to cross-border workflow design and developer integration.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt worked on ACCESS Next Generation from **2009 to 2012**. The bank was consolidating regional treasury systems into a global portal, but Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform needed custom payment modules, security controls, and workflows for **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. Each payment type had distinct formatting, validation, compliance, and settlement requirements.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore, spending **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and federal tax payment modules. His work included NACHA file validation, Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, risk-based approval controls, and real-time global reporting. He also led payments data migration, preserving client configurations, transaction histories, and compliance traceability **without disruption to live payment operations**. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**.

At **RBC**, fragmented systems and manual processes were delaying cross-border and bulk payments. Matt designed end-to-end workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation, partnering with the FX team on real-time currency conversion and transaction visibility. He delivered an implementation blueprint covering automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer, and batch processing. Revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire-transfer delays.

At **American Express**, adoption of its Virtual Payments Platform was slowed by missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox. Matt helped create a developer portal, Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, use-case-driven documentation, and secure virtualized testing environments. His team used Lean Product and XP practices and validated the portal through a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months**, onboarding time fell, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by **over 261 story points**.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes leading: empathy, clarity, and purpose, with decisions pushed to the people closest to the work.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, engineers, designers, and product teams were often coming from legacy command-and-control delivery cultures. Teams were over-processed, under-trusted, and waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes. As the centers scaled to **150+ practitioners**, some team members still hesitated to share ideas or take risks because they feared blame.

Matt addressed that through a “permit to fail” learning environment. He organized non-punitive post-mortems, focused discussions on lessons rather than pointing fingers, and supported low-stakes experiments with structured hypotheses and controlled iterations. He also shared his own experiences with mistakes and risk-taking. Team members began voicing concerns, proposing ideas, and experimenting more freely. Repeat failure patterns declined, morale improved, and turnover fell.

He organized balanced teams with engineers, product managers, and UX architects participating equally and sharing accountability. Instead of passing work between role silos, teams used pair programming, collaborative coding, regular retrospectives, and knowledge-sharing sessions. They could identify roadblocks and implement changes autonomously. Those changes reduced handoffs and project delays, improved team satisfaction and retention, and produced **zero-defect production code** across client engagements.

Matt also made intent explicit and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks, while grounding their work in automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices. At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a concrete example from **Norfolk Southern**.

In **2020**, Matt’s Cloud Innovation Center team was modernizing the client’s Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months into the engagement, just as the pandemic forced everyone into remote work, the client reported rising defects. The team’s dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The discrepancy surfaced in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and shared the gaps openly. An engineer had been coding from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests afterward. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Rather than treating it only as an individual performance issue, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. Engineers practiced through boot camps, coding katas, and pairing with subject-matter experts using an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

He also restructured agile ceremonies to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers working from the same requirements, supported by product management and SMART story training.

Defect rates dropped as test-first discipline took hold. **Norfolk Southern** stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and client and account leadership confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

During the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement, the team was modernizing the railroad’s legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A few months in, the client reported rising defects, even though the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, just as the pandemic forced the team into remote work.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Instead of simply telling engineers to follow the process, Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work alongside the team. They redid the code and tests, then reinforced the practices through boot camps, coding katas, and an “I do, we do, you do” progression.

He followed through after the experts left. Engineers rotated pairs daily, new engineers worked with seasoned practitioners, and writing test cases became an explicit step before building the solution, checked at standup. During remote work, pairs traded drivers frequently.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Pairing and test-first remained the team’s default after the experts went home, and the failure mode that caused the crisis did not recur.

He paired that environment with engineering rigor: automation, continuous delivery, quality-first practices, and balanced teams bringing product managers, designers, and engineers together. Teams delivered thin-slice, production-ready solutions to get user feedback, supported by workshops so client teams could continue the practices.

At the **150-person** Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. Teams also reported fewer repeat errors and shorter delivery timelines after adopting the learning-focused practices.

🐾 Here’s where Matt’s payments work went deepest.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt worked on ACCESS Next Generation from **2009 to 2012**. The bank was consolidating regional treasury systems into a global portal, but Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform did not provide all the payment modules, security controls, or connectivity required. Regional systems had different data models, entitlement structures, message formats, and compliance requirements, and live payments had to continue throughout the transition.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a **40+ person** blended **Accenture** and **JP Morgan Chase** team across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He defined the onshore-offshore engagement model and spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded with Bottomline’s team in Portsmouth, coordinating with bank stakeholders in Chicago and NY/NJ. He managed the build-versus-configure boundary: what WebSeries could handle and what required custom engineering.

His scope included ACH credits and direct debits, Fedwire and international wires, FX/cross-border payments, and federal tax payments. He also delivered payment verification through Message Authentication Codes, payment-type-specific permissions, sanctions screening, and connections to internal transaction monitoring. The centralized gateway handled message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**.

Matt also led payments data migration, working with compliance teams to preserve client configurations, transaction histories, and regulatory traceability. He owned production incident response, cross-team root-cause analysis, and daily leadership calls during live issues. ACCESS launched in **April 2011**, serving **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**; the migration completed without disruption to live payment operations.

At **American Express**, his later work focused on Virtual Payments Platform adoption. Missing SDKs, fragmented documentation, and no sandbox were slowing integration. Matt brought business and technical teams together through discovery workshops, introduced virtualized testing environments, and led developer-portal improvements, cross-stack SDKs, and use-case-driven documentation. API trial usage increased within **3 months**, onboarding time fell, and the team exceeded its delivery commitment by over **261 story points**.

Environment virtualization let developers test earlier without waiting on downstream dependencies. Delivery stabilized within **3 months**. Matt recovered a release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **\$500K** in penalties. answer_md:
🐾 Found it! Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here’s how Matt changed the team’s day-to-day work.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working through **6-month** waterfall release cycles, with requirements buried in a **200-page** BRD organized by system modules. Developers in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland had no visibility into work status. Deadlines kept slipping, client stakeholders were threatening cancellation, and PMO and compliance teams resisted the move to agile.

Matt decomposed the BRD into persona-based user stories rather than system-module tasks. He replaced a single To Do/Done JIRA board with a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture, tracking the **47** acceptance criteria as Epics and moving stories through specific workflow columns. He established follow-the-sun synchronization: a **7 AM** CST scrum-of-scrums for offshore-to-onshore handoffs and **11 PM** CST syncs for the reverse handoff.

He introduced bi-weekly sprint demos so stakeholders could sign off on branding, UI, and ADA compliance early instead of discovering issues at month **6**. When stakeholders lacked time for that feedback cadence, he negotiated dedicated review windows. He maintained steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility. For PMO and compliance, he used JIRA audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments instead of static Word documents. He also coached offshore teams on empowerment over command-and-control and put screen reader audits into the Definition of Done.

Alongside that working-model change, Matt introduced mandatory senior-developer code reviews, unit tests tied to backlog stories, and automated build quality gates. He coordinated **3** external vendors across payment processing, fraud detection, and hosting to resolve dependencies.

The team moved to **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. JIRA gave **50+** stakeholders visibility across **3** time zones and satisfied PMO and compliance audit requirements. The program met **47** acceptance criteria with **zero** critical defects at launch.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s Matt’s **RBC** work.

From **June 2012 to June 2013**, Matt worked as a Senior Technology Architecture Manager on **RBC’s** commercial banking modernization. The bank was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine for its Day**2Day** Corporate Banking platform, replacing the aging **RBC Express** portal. Existing systems had performance and scalability limitations, lacked mobile capabilities, and had no API integration with external financial applications.

A central question was whether the proposed platform could actually meet the bank’s requirements. Matt assessed Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture, conducted code reviews and interviews, and created architectural heat maps comparing requirements with WebSeries capabilities. He worked with the bank’s enterprise architecture team on target-system models and a cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity required for **RBC’s** long-term digital operating model. That finding prevented further investment in a platform path that could not deliver and enabled resources to move to higher-priority initiatives.

Alongside that assessment, Matt established the PMO across **RBC**, **Accenture**, and Bottomline Technologies. He introduced centralized updates, designated team contacts, a task-tracking matrix, and risk and dependency reporting. The communication framework eliminated missed program updates, while the task matrix reduced duplicate effort.

When the previous data conversion lead left, Matt took over planning from scratch. He analyzed legacy payment records, documented source-to-target transformation rules, planned mock conversion cycles, and established reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details. He also published and presented a migration strategy that **RBC** adopted.

For mobile banking, Matt defined API integration points, cheque deposit requirements, and cross-browser and cross-device scalability needs. The deliverable was a modernization blueprint for mobile adoption and real-time account access, not a reported mobile product launch.

When the original JSP-only architecture became fragile and slow, he learned MVC and refactored the live product onto servlets and beans.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what connects Matt’s work across delivery, organizational transformation, and talent development.

Across his engagements, modernization often ran into unchanged ways of working. Clients hired teams to replace technology but kept the same silos, handoffs, and bottlenecks. At **Norfolk Southern**, the mainframe modernization also faced a client organization shaped around mainframe thinking, account leadership accustomed to waterfall, and a delivery team learning new practices. At **American Express**, dependency bottlenecks, delayed testing, and poor documentation slowed integration with the Virtual Payments Platform. In both engagements, teams needed changes to how they worked alongside changes to the systems they built.

Matt brought business and technical contributors into the work together. At **Norfolk Southern**, he led domain-driven design and event storming sessions, then brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create when the client grew restless for tangible progress. The mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB rose beside it. Weekly build-measure-learn iterations gave the client working increments to review. The MVP launched covering **95%** of its targeted use cases.

He also changed the conditions around delivery. At **American Express**, Matt introduced environment virtualization so developers could test earlier without waiting on downstream dependencies. He paired that with a redesigned portal, updated documentation, and Lean Product and XP practices. The team delivered over **261 additional story points** of customer-focused value.

Coaching happened inside the work rather than separately from it. At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt used “I do, we do, you do,” pairing scarce domain experts with team members and rotating their knowledge through the team. Client contributors also paired into the new-state build, learning the technologies needed to support it after **Accenture** rolled off.

Across broader transformation engagements, Matt restructured teams around business domains and coached leadership toward product-centric operating models. Clients adopted self-regulating balanced teams and lean product practices that outlasted the engagements, with cost reductions of **15-35%**. Within the CIC, balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects used iterative development and real-time feedback loops to achieve zero-defect production code.

Across the engineering engagements described, teams reached **4X velocity** compared with client internal teams doing equivalent work after the initial learning curve.
